What does a yes vote on Proposition 5 mean?
Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
What does a no vote on Proposition 5 mean?
Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
What would Proposition 5 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says the net effect is unknown. Separate special elections could cost millions of dollars each, while dropping replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions. The Analyst says these costs or savings would be rare and depend on which office is recalled.
What it means for the City of LA
Proposition 5 covers only state officers: the Governor, other statewide officials, legislators and certain judges. Recalls of the Mayor, City Council members and other City officials follow the City Charter, which puts the recall question and the election of a successor on the same ballot; Proposition 5 does not change that. City residents would still vote in any state recall, and Los Angeles County's cost for the 2021 Governor recall was $52.9 million.
The details
Official title Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Legislative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the Legislature (SCA 1, Resolution Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. Under the State Constitution (Article XVIII, Section 4), an amendment takes effect if "approved by a majority of votes cast thereon."
The question on your ballot
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
This is not the Proposition 5 on the November 5, 2024 ballot, the measure on local bonds for affordable housing and infrastructure, which failed with 45.0% voting yes (Secretary of State, November 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-general/sov/59-state-ballot-measures.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 5 passes
Recall ballot Two questions: remove the official, and who replaces them if removed (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)) One question: remove the official or not (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Who takes office after a recall The replacement candidate with the most votes, even without a majority (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)) The office becomes vacant and is filled under existing vacancy rules (text, Art. II, Sec. 15(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Recalled Governor Replaced by the top replacement candidate The Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor. If the recall comes before the nomination period closes for the next statewide election in the first two years of the term, a special election is held with the next statewide primary, and a runoff at the general election if no one gets a majority. Otherwise the Lieutenant Governor serves out the term (text, Art. V, Sec. 10(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Recalled legislator Replaced by the top replacement candidate Seat filled by a special election called by the Governor (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Other recalled state officers (e.g. Attorney General) Replaced by the top replacement candidate Governor appoints a replacement under existing vacancy rules (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Can the recalled official run again? May not be a candidate to replace themselves (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf)) May run in the later special election, but may not be appointed to the seat (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/title-summary.htm); text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
The rules for qualifying a recall, such as signature counts and deadlines, do not change. A recall election must still be held 60 to 80 days after signatures are certified, or within 180 days if combined with a regular election (text, Art. II, Sec. 15 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
City recalls are not affected. Proposition 5 amends only Sections 15 and 17 of Article II and Section 10 of Article V of the State Constitution, which cover state officers (SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1); LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)). Recalls of City officials follow the City Charter. When a City recall petition qualifies, the Council calls an election on whether to recall the officer “and if recalled, for the election of his or her successor” (City Clerk petition handbook, p. 21, citing Charter sec. 432 (https://clerk.lacity.gov/sites/g/files/wph1491/files/2021-03/lacityp_023253.pdf#page=21)). That two-part City process stays the same.
City voters and state recalls. City residents vote in any statewide recall and in recalls of legislators who represent them. In the 2021 Governor recall, Los Angeles County voters opposed removal 70.8% to 29.2% (Statement of Vote, recall question (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/16-question.pdf)).
Election costs. County election offices run state recalls. Los Angeles County reported $52,920,735 in costs for the 2021 recall, against a state allocation of $59,793,000 (Secretary of State cost report (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/report-to-legislature.pdf)). The Analyst says Proposition 5 could raise or lower future recall costs and that the split between the state and counties “would depend on future decisions by the Legislature” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)).
We found no City Council or City Clerk position on Proposition 5 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
A constitutional amendment written by the Legislature needs a two-thirds vote of each house (SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Jan. 30, 2023: Sen. Josh Newman introduced SCA 1. Assemblymember Isaac Bryan was the principal coauthor (SCA 1 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1); SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Feb. 1, 2024: The Senate adopted it 31-7 (SCA 1 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Aug. 30-31, 2024: The Assembly adopted the amended version 59-17 and the Senate agreed 32-8 (SCA 1 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)). The Senate no votes were Alvarado-Gil, Dahle, Grove, Jones, Nguyen, Niello, Ochoa Bogh and Seyarto.
Sept. 10, 2024: Filed with the Secretary of State as Resolution Chapter 204 (SCA 1 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)). It appears on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot (SOS voter guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/)).
The 2018 recall of the measure’s author. Newman was recalled from the 29th Senate District in 2018, and Republican Ling Ling Chang was elected his successor on the same ballot (Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)). The Daily News reports the recall passed 58% to 42% after Newman voted for a gas tax increase in 2017, and that he won the seat back in 2020 (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/08/12/endorsement-vote-no-on-proposition-5-an-attack-on-californias-recall-power/)). The Sacramento Bee reports Chang won with just under 34% of the vote (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/proposition-5-could-change-california-s-recall-elections-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2cxbHa)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. A constitutional amendment “if approved by a majority of votes cast thereon, takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
Recall history. Since 1913, 11 state recalls have qualified for the ballot, nine against legislators and two against Governors, and six officials were removed (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm); Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)). Two of the qualified recalls, both in 1994, targeted Los Angeles County legislators: Sen. David Roberti, who kept his seat, and Assemblyman Paul Horcher, who was removed (Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm)). No supporters or opponents were listed on the ballot label (ballot label (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/)).
Argument in favor, signed by Lorrel Plimier of the League of Women Voters of California, Darius L. Kemp of California Common Cause and former FPPC chair Dan Schnur (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
The two linked questions are “a dangerous loophole”: an official can be removed by a narrow majority and replaced by someone with “far less than 50%.”
The 2021 recall “lost by nearly the same number of votes that the Governor won the regular election with” and cost “more than $200 million.”
Had the 2021 recall succeeded, the leading replacement would have taken office “with support from only about 28% of all recall voters.”
“In most states with recalls, vacancies are already filled by succession or a separate election.”
Argument against, signed by Senate Minority Leader Brian W. Jones and Assemblymember Joe Patterson (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
It takes away voters’ power to choose a replacement. In many cases, it says, politicians rather than voters would choose who fills the vacancy.
Seats could sit vacant until “another costly election.”
The recalled official could run in the next election.
The measure’s author was recalled by voters after he voted to raise gas taxes.
Outside the guide.
Carl DeMaio, who led the 2017-18 Newman recall, told the Sacramento Bee editorial board that politicians facing a recall could say “you won’t be represented for 12 months” (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/proposition-5-could-change-california-s-recall-elections-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2cxbHa)).
Newman told the Bee: “So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in’” (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/proposition-5-could-change-california-s-recall-elections-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2cxbHa)).
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association says the measure “makes a mockery of the recall process” (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)).

The 2021 recall cost more than $200 million Yes campaign The Secretary of State reported a total cost of $200,241,680: $174,059,031.11 for counties and $26,182,649.08 for the state (cost report (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/report-to-legislature.pdf)).
The 2021 recall lost by about the margin Newsom won by in 2018 Yes campaign Recall question: 38.1% yes, 61.9% no (Statement of Vote, 2021 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/16-question.pdf)). 2018 Governor: Newsom 61.9%, John Cox 38.1% (Statement of Vote, 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-general/sov/07-summary.pdf)).
The leading replacement would have won with about 28% of recall voters Yes campaign Larry Elder led with 3,563,867 votes, 48.4% of replacement votes (Statement of Vote, replacement candidates (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/20-replacement-candidates.pdf)). That is 27.8% of the 12,838,565 votes cast on the recall question (our calculation).
Politicians would choose the replacement No campaign True for statewide offices other than Governor and Lieutenant Governor succession: the Governor appoints. Legislative seats go to a special election, and a recalled Governor is succeeded by the elected Lieutenant Governor (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)).
The recalled official could run again No campaign Yes, in the later special election; the official could not be appointed (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/title-summary.htm)).
Special elections cost more No campaign The Analyst says a standalone special election “could be millions of dollars,” and that dropping the second question could also save millions (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)).
We did not check the “nearly 70% of likely voters called the effort a waste” figure or the claim about recall rules in other states.

percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.

Californians and Their GovernmentOctober 2026
Full Crosstabs–Likely Voters Only
Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in
English and Spanish according to the respondents’ preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place
from October 16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8
percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.
If you have any questions or require additional information regarding this survey, please contact surveys@ppic.org

From left: Jill Replogle, Destiny Torres, Jon Gould and Michael Moodian.
Dean Jon Gould breaks it down at LAist cram session
By Mimi Ko Cruz (mailto:mkcruz@uci.edu)
Jon Gould broke it down for the Orange County voters who packed a Corona del Mar senior center on Oct. 13: the ballot is long, the propositions are complicated, some of them designed that way on purpose.
The dean of UC Irvine’s School of Social Ecology was a featured expert at the LAist Orange County Ballot Cram Session, a free event hosted by reporters Jill Replogle and Destiny Torres at the OASIS Senior Center. Gould and Michael Moodian of Chapman University walked the audience through 13 statewide propositions, two Board of Supervisors runoffs, and a ranked choice voting measure in Irvine — pulling no punches along the way.
Here is a rundown of the statewide measures:
Proposition 1 – Affordable Housing Bond , authorizes $11.25 billion in bonds for affordable housing, with $1.25 billion set aside for veterans. Gould called it “one of the most straightforward propositions on the ballot,” but cautioned that the veteran angle is somewhat overstated. “This is really less about veterans than it is about general affordable housing in California,” he said. Polling at around 55 percent.
Proposition 2 – Rainy Day Fund , would raise the cap on how much of the state’s general fund can be saved, from 10% to 20%. Gould noted it has unusual bipartisan support — Newsom and the legislative Democrats back it, but so does the Los Angeles Chamber of Commerce and firefighters. Polling at about 60%, which Gould said makes it likely to pass. When asked if it would ease the strain on local budgets, Gould was succinct: “No. Full stop.”
Proposition 3 – High Income Tax Rate Made Permanent , would make permanent the income tax surcharge on high earners — roughly those making more than $370,000 for single filers — that voters first passed in 2012 and extended in 2016. If it expires in 2031, the highest rate of 12.3% would drop to around 9%. About 89% of revenues go to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges. Polling at 58%. Replogle offered this context: “If this gets rejected and the tax rate goes back to what it was before 2012 for those highest income earners, someone who makes $3 million a year would be taxed at the same rate as somebody who makes $73,000 a year.”
Proposition 4 – Public Funding for Elections , would allow state and non-charter local governments to use taxpayer money to fund candidate campaigns, a system already in place in about five or six charter cities including Berkeley. Polling poorly — 42% in one survey, 35% in another. Gould said voters appear to be reacting viscerally: “Ugh, politicians, I don’t want to spend money on them.” Supported by the League of Women Voters and Common Cause but largely flying under the radar.
Proposition 5 – Recall Reform , would separate the question of recalling an official from the vote to replace them, requiring a special election for any successor. Gould traced the issue back to the Josh Newman and Gray Davis recalls, where replacement candidates won with as little as 30 to 33% of the vote. “I don’t see this winning,” Gould said. Not polling well, and opposed by the Republican Party.
Proposition 37 – Home Buyer Loan Assistance , a $25 billion revenue bond program offering middle-income buyers a fixed-rate second mortgage of up to 17% of a new home’s price, with buyers still required to put 3% down. The state would essentially act as a mortgage broker, Gould said. “People who want a house who can’t afford a house are not spending a whole lot of time asking about the geopolitical or larger economic issues. They’re asking, how can I afford a house?” Strongly backed by realtors and the construction industry. Polling well, with Gould calling it “probably passable,” though he noted buyers would be leveraged at 97% of their home's value.
Proposition 38 – Medical Research Bond , an $8.4 billion bond for cancer, Alzheimer’s, and other disease research. Half the money would go to a specific UCLA-affiliated institute backed by the proposition’s primary funder, Gary Michaelson, who has put in $43 million of the $51 million raised, Moodian said. Gould declined to comment directly, saying simply, “Since I am employed by the University of California, I’m going to say nothing.”
Proposition 39 – Voter ID , would require government-issued photo ID at the polls and the last four digits of an ID on mail-in ballots, and direct election officials to cross-check voter rolls with citizenship data. “There is simply no evidence anywhere in America of widespread voter fraud. There just isn’t,” Gould said, though he acknowledged a secondary argument, that showing ID adds a sense of civic integrity to voting. California-based pollsters show it failing by large margins; some out-of-state pollsters show it winning. Gould said it is one to watch on election night. Driven by the California Republican Party and opposed by Democrats.
Proposition 40 – One-Time Billionaire Tax , would impose a 5% tax on the assets — not income — of Californians with a net worth over $1 billion. Revenues would go primarily to healthcare, with some going to education and food assistance. Despite what would seem like a politically easy sell, it is currently polling below 50%. “This goes against everything I thought I knew about political science,” Gould said. “I thought voters would say, ‘Oh my God, we need money. It’s going to education. It’s going to healthcare. And it’s billionaires — sign me up.’ And, at the moment, it sure doesn’t look like that.” Supported by Senator Bernie Sanders; opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom and establishment Democrats.
Proposition 41 – Pre-Vote Tax Audit Requirement , would require the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. Gould said this is the most technically difficult proposition to understand, but the cleaner way to grasp it is this: a yes on 41 is effectively a no on Prop. 40, since it would nullify the billionaire tax if both pass. Funded heavily by billionaires opposing Prop. 40. Currently polling worse than Prop. 40 itself.
Proposition 42 – Ban on Personal Property Taxes , would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — not real estate — and ban retroactive taxes. Like Prop. 41, it is designed to undercut Prop. 40, and is heavily funded by tech billionaires including Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Gould noted that it has produced its own strange political coalition: technology investors and business groups are aligned with construction trade unions, firefighters and police, who are worried about retirement accounts. “If you are confused, that was intentional by the people who wrote 41 and 42, because they are trying to muddy the waters on 40.”
Proposition 43 – Two-Thirds Threshold for Local Special Taxes , would require a two-thirds voter approval for citizen-initiated local special taxes, up from a simple majority. Already failing badly in polling. Gould noted an irony: though it sounds like a citizen-led idea, it was placed on the ballot by the legislature in a deal to head off something more restrictive from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.
Proposition 44 – Community Clinic Spending Rule , would require nonprofit community health clinics to spend 90% of their revenues on direct patient care or face fines. Currently losing 2-to-1 in the only available poll.
Proposition 45 – CEQA Reform , would impose roughly a one-year deadline on environmental reviews and legal challenges for so-called essential projects including housing, roads, schools, broadband, and wildfire mitigation. Orange County Board of Supervisors races
On the Board of Supervisors, Gould called the District 5 race between incumbent Democrat Katrina Foley and former Newport Beach Mayor Diane Dixon “probably the most competitive of any of the races we are going to see in Orange County in 2026.”
He pointed to a notable wrinkle: outgoing Democratic supervisor Doug Chaffee has not endorsed Foley and is listed as a supporter on Dixon's website — a move Gould called “the controversy that is hiding in plain sight in this race.”
Foley has out-raised Dixon roughly 3 to 1, pulling in about $3 million largely from public employee and police and fire unions.
In District 4, which covers Brea, Fullerton, and parts of Anaheim, Democrat Connor Trout faces Republican Tim Shaw for the seat being vacated by Chaffee.
Democrats hold a roughly 10-point registration advantage in the district, though Gould cautioned that advantage has not always translated into wins.
Ranked choice voting
The panel closed with a discussion of an Irvine initiative to adopt ranked choice voting for city council and mayoral races — a measure endorsed by the Irvine mayor and opposed by the vice mayor. Gould said if it passes and voters embrace it, it could become a model for other California cities.

### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

## Opponents argue this initiative strips power from citizens and hands it directly to Sacramento political insiders
By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:32 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST
**Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...**
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement.
In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy.
In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.

### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

Voters get their say with Prop. 5 by Kate Wolffe (https://calmatters.org/author/kate-wolffe/) October 5, 2026 October 2, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-5-explainer/) Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-5-explainer/) Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-5-explainer/) Then-gubernatorial candidate Arnold Schwarzenegger celebrates his victory in the California recall election with his wife Maria Shriver at the Century Plaza Hotel in Los Angeles, on Oct. 7, 2003. Photo by NewsBase via AP Photo In summary Following the failed 2021 recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom, Democrats had the political will and momentum to call for changes to the recall process. What emerged was Proposition 5 on the November ballot, a measure to change the recall process. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. Sign up for free Δ “We’ve identified that weak gazelle, the slowest gazelle, the one with the limp,” he said. “And that’s Josh Newman, in Orange County.” Why Newman? Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate. Gov. Gray Davis speaks at an anti-recall labor union rally in San Jose on Oct. 5, 2003. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. Proposition 5 : Change how recalled state officials are replaced
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 5 would remove the second question from state recall elections, the one asking who should replace the official if recalled. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor, either for the rest of the term or until voters elect a new Governor, depending on timing. Other recalled offices would be filled the way vacancies are filled now: a special election for legislators and appointment by the Governor for most other offices.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 5 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 5
What changes State recall ballots would ask only whether to remove the official; no replacement candidates
Who fills a recalled Governor's seat The Lieutenant Governor, for the rest of the term or until a special election, depending on timing
Vote needed Simple majority
Legislature's vote Senate 32-8, Assembly 59-17 (August 2024)
Money No committee primarily formed for or against it. Against: $40,500 in outside spending by Reform California (shared with other props)
Latest public poll PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 45% yes, 52% no (likely voters)
Each figure is sourced in the sections below.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , The details , How it got on the ballot , What would change , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 5 mean?
Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
What does a no vote on Proposition 5 mean?
Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
What would Proposition 5 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says the net effect is unknown. Separate special elections could cost millions of dollars each, while dropping replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions. The Analyst says these costs or savings would be rare and depend on which office is recalled.
What it means for the City of LA
Proposition 5 covers only state officers: the Governor, other statewide officials, legislators and certain judges. Recalls of the Mayor, City Council members and other City officials follow the City Charter, which puts the recall question and the election of a successor on the same ballot; Proposition 5 does not change that. City residents would still vote in any state recall, and Los Angeles County's cost for the 2021 Governor recall was $52.9 million.
The details
Official title Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Legislative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the Legislature (SCA 1, Resolution Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. Under the State Constitution (Article XVIII, Section 4), an amendment takes effect if "approved by a majority of votes cast thereon."
The question on your ballot
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
This is not the Proposition 5 on the November 5, 2024 ballot, the measure on local bonds for affordable housing and infrastructure, which failed with 45.0% voting yes (Secretary of State, November 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-general/sov/59-state-ballot-measures.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 5 passes
Recall ballot Two questions: remove the official, and who replaces them if removed (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)) One question: remove the official or not (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Who takes office after a recall The replacement candidate with the most votes, even without a majority (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)) The office becomes vacant and is filled under existing vacancy rules (text, Art. II, Sec. 15(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Recalled Governor Replaced by the top replacement candidate The Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor. If the recall comes before the nomination period closes for the next statewide election in the first two years of the term, a special election is held with the next statewide primary, and a runoff at the general election if no one gets a majority. Otherwise the Lieutenant Governor serves out the term (text, Art. V, Sec. 10(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Recalled legislator Replaced by the top replacement candidate Seat filled by a special election called by the Governor (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Other recalled state officers (e.g. Attorney General) Replaced by the top replacement candidate Governor appoints a replacement under existing vacancy rules (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Can the recalled official run again? May not be a candidate to replace themselves (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf)) May run in the later special election, but may not be appointed to the seat (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/title-summary.htm); text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
The rules for qualifying a recall, such as signature counts and deadlines, do not change. A recall election must still be held 60 to 80 days after signatures are certified, or within 180 days if combined with a regular election (text, Art. II, Sec. 15 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
City recalls are not affected. Proposition 5 amends only Sections 15 and 17 of Article II and Section 10 of Article V of the State Constitution, which cover state officers (SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1); LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)). Recalls of City officials follow the City Charter. When a City recall petition qualifies, the Council calls an election on whether to recall the officer “and if recalled, for the election of his or her successor” (City Clerk petition handbook, p. 21, citing Charter sec. 432 (https://clerk.lacity.gov/sites/g/files/wph1491/files/2021-03/lacityp_023253.pdf#page=21)). That two-part City process stays the same.
City voters and state recalls. City residents vote in any statewide recall and in recalls of legislators who represent them. In the 2021 Governor recall, Los Angeles County voters opposed removal 70.8% to 29.2% (Statement of Vote, recall question (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/16-question.pdf)).
Election costs. County election offices run state recalls. Los Angeles County reported $52,920,735 in costs for the 2021 recall, against a state allocation of $59,793,000 (Secretary of State cost report (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/report-to-legislature.pdf)). The Analyst says Proposition 5 could raise or lower future recall costs and that the split between the state and counties “would depend on future decisions by the Legislature” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)).
We found no City Council or City Clerk position on Proposition 5 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
A constitutional amendment written by the Legislature needs a two-thirds vote of each house (SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Jan. 30, 2023: Sen. Josh Newman introduced SCA 1. Assemblymember Isaac Bryan was the principal coauthor (SCA 1 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1); SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Feb. 1, 2024: The Senate adopted it 31-7 (SCA 1 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Aug. 30-31, 2024: The Assembly adopted the amended version 59-17 and the Senate agreed 32-8 (SCA 1 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)). The Senate no votes were Alvarado-Gil, Dahle, Grove, Jones, Nguyen, Niello, Ochoa Bogh and Seyarto.
Sept. 10, 2024: Filed with the Secretary of State as Resolution Chapter 204 (SCA 1 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)). It appears on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot (SOS voter guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/)).
The 2018 recall of the measure’s author. Newman was recalled from the 29th Senate District in 2018, and Republican Ling Ling Chang was elected his successor on the same ballot (Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)). The Daily News reports the recall passed 58% to 42% after Newman voted for a gas tax increase in 2017, and that he won the seat back in 2020 (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/08/12/endorsement-vote-no-on-proposition-5-an-attack-on-californias-recall-power/)). The Sacramento Bee reports Chang won with just under 34% of the vote (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/proposition-5-could-change-california-s-recall-elections-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2cxbHa)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. A constitutional amendment “if approved by a majority of votes cast thereon, takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
Recall history. Since 1913, 11 state recalls have qualified for the ballot, nine against legislators and two against Governors, and six officials were removed (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm); Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)). Two of the qualified recalls, both in 1994, targeted Los Angeles County legislators: Sen. David Roberti, who kept his seat, and Assemblyman Paul Horcher, who was removed (Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/arguments-rebuttals.htm)). No supporters or opponents were listed on the ballot label (ballot label (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/)).

Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in
English and Spanish according to the respondents’ preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place
from October 16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8
percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.
If you have any questions or require additional information regarding this survey, please contact surveys@ppic.org

Voters face ballot full of traps, tricks and trillion-dollar stakes
Oct
15
2026
October 15, 2026
From left: Jill Replogle, Destiny Torres, Jon Gould and Michael Moodian.
Dean Jon Gould breaks it down at LAist cram session
By Mimi Ko Cruz (mailto:mkcruz@uci.edu)
Jon Gould broke it down for the Orange County voters who packed a Corona del Mar senior center on Oct. 13: the ballot is long, the propositions are complicated, some of them designed that way on purpose.
The dean of UC Irvine’s School of Social Ecology was a featured expert at the LAist Orange County Ballot Cram Session, a free event hosted by reporters Jill Replogle and Destiny Torres at the OASIS Senior Center. Gould and Michael Moodian of Chapman University walked the audience through 13 statewide propositions, two Board of Supervisors runoffs, and a ranked choice voting measure in Irvine — pulling no punches along the way.
Here is a rundown of the statewide measures:
Proposition 1 – Affordable Housing Bond , authorizes $11.25 billion in bonds for affordable housing, with $1.25 billion set aside for veterans. Gould called it “one of the most straightforward propositions on the ballot,” but cautioned that the veteran angle is somewhat overstated. “This is really less about veterans than it is about general affordable housing in California,” he said. Polling at around 55 percent.
Proposition 2 – Rainy Day Fund , would raise the cap on how much of the state’s general fund can be saved, from 10% to 20%. Gould noted it has unusual bipartisan support — Newsom and the legislative Democrats back it, but so does the Los Angeles Chamber of Commerce and firefighters. Polling at about 60%, which Gould said makes it likely to pass. When asked if it would ease the strain on local budgets, Gould was succinct: “No. Full stop.”
Proposition 3 – High Income Tax Rate Made Permanent , would make permanent the income tax surcharge on high earners — roughly those making more than $370,000 for single filers — that voters first passed in 2012 and extended in 2016. If it expires in 2031, the highest rate of 12.3% would drop to around 9%. About 89% of revenues go to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges. Polling at 58%. Replogle offered this context: “If this gets rejected and the tax rate goes back to what it was before 2012 for those highest income earners, someone who makes $3 million a year would be taxed at the same rate as somebody who makes $73,000 a year.”
Proposition 4 – Public Funding for Elections , would allow state and non-charter local governments to use taxpayer money to fund candidate campaigns, a system already in place in about five or six charter cities including Berkeley. Polling poorly — 42% in one survey, 35% in another. Gould said voters appear to be reacting viscerally: “Ugh, politicians, I don’t want to spend money on them.” Supported by the League of Women Voters and Common Cause but largely flying under the radar.
Proposition 5 – Recall Reform , would separate the question of recalling an official from the vote to replace them, requiring a special election for any successor. Gould traced the issue back to the Josh Newman and Gray Davis recalls, where replacement candidates won with as little as 30 to 33% of the vote. “I don’t see this winning,” Gould said. Not polling well, and opposed by the Republican Party.
Proposition 37 – Home Buyer Loan Assistance , a $25 billion revenue bond program offering middle-income buyers a fixed-rate second mortgage of up to 17% of a new home’s price, with buyers still required to put 3% down. The state would essentially act as a mortgage broker, Gould said. “People who want a house who can’t afford a house are not spending a whole lot of time asking about the geopolitical or larger economic issues. They’re asking, how can I afford a house?” Strongly backed by realtors and the construction industry. Polling well, with Gould calling it “probably passable,” though he noted buyers would be leveraged at 97% of their home's value.
Proposition 38 – Medical Research Bond , an $8.4 billion bond for cancer, Alzheimer’s, and other disease research. Half the money would go to a specific UCLA-affiliated institute backed by the proposition’s primary funder, Gary Michaelson, who has put in $43 million of the $51 million raised, Moodian said. Gould declined to comment directly, saying simply, “Since I am employed by the University of California, I’m going to say nothing.”
Proposition 39 – Voter ID , would require government-issued photo ID at the polls and the last four digits of an ID on mail-in ballots, and direct election officials to cross-check voter rolls with citizenship data. “There is simply no evidence anywhere in America of widespread voter fraud. There just isn’t,” Gould said, though he acknowledged a secondary argument, that showing ID adds a sense of civic integrity to voting. California-based pollsters show it failing by large margins; some out-of-state pollsters show it winning. Gould said it is one to watch on election night. Driven by the California Republican Party and opposed by Democrats.
Proposition 40 – One-Time Billionaire Tax , would impose a 5% tax on the assets — not income — of Californians with a net worth over $1 billion. Revenues would go primarily to healthcare, with some going to education and food assistance. Despite what would seem like a politically easy sell, it is currently polling below 50%. “This goes against everything I thought I knew about political science,” Gould said. “I thought voters would say, ‘Oh my God, we need money. It’s going to education. It’s going to healthcare. And it’s billionaires — sign me up.’ And, at the moment, it sure doesn’t look like that.” Supported by Senator Bernie Sanders; opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom and establishment Democrats.
Proposition 41 – Pre-Vote Tax Audit Requirement , would require the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters. Gould said this is the most technically difficult proposition to understand, but the cleaner way to grasp it is this: a yes on 41 is effectively a no on Prop. 40, since it would nullify the billionaire tax if both pass. Funded heavily by billionaires opposing Prop. 40. Currently polling worse than Prop. 40 itself.
Proposition 42 – Ban on Personal Property Taxes , would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — not real estate — and ban retroactive taxes. Like Prop. 41, it is designed to undercut Prop. 40, and is heavily funded by tech billionaires including Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Gould noted that it has produced its own strange political coalition: technology investors and business groups are aligned with construction trade unions, firefighters and police, who are worried about retirement accounts. “If you are confused, that was intentional by the people who wrote 41 and 42, because they are trying to muddy the waters on 40.”
Proposition 43 – Two-Thirds Threshold for Local Special Taxes , would require a two-thirds voter approval for citizen-initiated local special taxes, up from a simple majority. Already failing badly in polling. Gould noted an irony: though it sounds like a citizen-led idea, it was placed on the ballot by the legislature in a deal to head off something more restrictive from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.
Proposition 44 – Community Clinic Spending Rule , would require nonprofit community health clinics to spend 90% of their revenues on direct patient care or face fines. Currently losing 2-to-1 in the only available poll.
Proposition 45 – CEQA Reform , would impose roughly a one-year deadline on environmental reviews and legal challenges for so-called essential projects including housing, roads, schools, broadband, and wildfire mitigation. Polling about 50-50. “If it weren’t for the housing crisis right now, I don’t think 45 would be on the ballot, and I don’t think it would pass,” Gould said. “But given the housing crisis that we’re having, this one’s really in play.” Supported by developers, utilities and the chambers of commerce; opposed by environmental groups and some labor unions.
Orange County Board of Supervisors races
On the Board of Supervisors, Gould called the District 5 race between incumbent Democrat Katrina Foley and former Newport Beach Mayor Diane Dixon “probably the most competitive of any of the races we are going to see in Orange County in 2026.”
He pointed to a notable wrinkle: outgoing Democratic supervisor Doug Chaffee has not endorsed Foley and is listed as a supporter on Dixon's website — a move Gould called “the controversy that is hiding in plain sight in this race.”
Foley has out-raised Dixon roughly 3 to 1, pulling in about $3 million largely from public employee and police and fire unions.
In District 4, which covers Brea, Fullerton, and parts of Anaheim, Democrat Connor Trout faces Republican Tim Shaw for the seat being vacated by Chaffee.
Democrats hold a roughly 10-point registration advantage in the district, though Gould cautioned that advantage has not always translated into wins.
Ranked choice voting
The panel closed with a discussion of an Irvine initiative to adopt ranked choice voting for city council and mayoral races — a measure endorsed by the Irvine mayor and opposed by the vice mayor. Gould said if it passes and voters embrace it, it could become a model for other California cities.

### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
CON
Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

October 12, 2026 / 6:06 PM PDT / CBS Sacramento
California voters will decide in November whether to overhaul the state's recall election process.
Proposition 5, authored by former Democratic state Sen.
Josh Newman, would change how California fills vacancies when state officials are recalled.
Under the current system, voters decide whether to remove an official and simultaneously select a potential replacement.
If approved, Proposition 5 would separate those decisions, with vacancies generally filled through subsequent special elections or appointments, depending on the office.
The measure also includes specific rules for replacing a governor and would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the position.
A September poll from the Public Policy Institute of California found that 59% of likely voters said they would vote against Proposition 5, while 35% said they would vote in favor.
Another 5% were undecided.
The measure will appear on California's Nov. 3, 2026, general election ballot.

## No
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Election of State Officials. The State Constitution establishes legislative, executive, and judicial state offices. Some state officials represent parts of the state, known as districts. Other state officials, like the Governor or Attorney General, represent the entire state. Voters elect people to represent them in state offices for set terms. For example, a state Assembly Member is elected to a two-year term and the Governor is elected to a four-year term. To run for a state office, candidates must submit specific nomination documents before the election. State law sets when this “nomination period” occurs.
Recall of State Officials. The State Constitution allows voters to remove state officials from office before their term ends through a recall. A recall is an election in which voters are asked whether to remove an official from office. To qualify a recall for the ballot, supporters of the recall must collect a certain number of signatures from the official’s district (or statewide for statewide offices). Since 1913, 11 state recall efforts have qualified for the ballot (nine legislators and two Governors) and six have resulted in an official’s removal from office (five legislators and one Governor).
Two Questions in Recall Elections. In a recall election, voters are asked two questions: (1) whether the official should be removed from office and (2) who should replace the official if removed from office. The number of candidates appearing in the second question varies. For example, there were 135 candidates in the 2003 Governor recall election and 46 candidates in the 2021 Governor recall election. If a state official is recalled, the person who receives the most votes in the second question assumes the office.
Vacant State Offices. State officials may leave office before the end of their term for reasons other than a recall. For example, they may die or resign. When this happens, the office becomes vacant. The process to fill a vacant office varies by office. Typically, a vacant seat in the Assembly or Senate is filled through a special election called by the Governor. The Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor when there is a vacancy in the office of the Governor. Vacancies in other executive offices (for example, the Lieutenant Governor or Attorney General) and the Supreme Court and Courts of Appeal are filled by appointments by the Governor.
Frequency of Elections. Statewide elections in California are scheduled every two years. In scheduled election years, a primary election is held in either March or June, depending on the year, and a general election is held in November. In addition to scheduled elections, the state and local governments may call special elections to address specific issues. For example, the Governor may call a special election to fill a vacant Assembly seat.
Elections Administration in California. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have election-related workload. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
Paying for State Recall Elections. State law requires the California Department of Finance to work with state and local elections officials to estimate the cost of a recall election for a state office. The department is required to send the estimate to the Legislature. The Legislature reviews the estimate and may provide funding for the election. Any remaining costs are paid by the Secretary of State’s and counties’ budgets.
PROPOSAL
As described below, Proposition 5 changes the recall process to make it like the existing process for filling vacant state offices, except for the process to recall the Governor.
Removes Second Question From Recall Elections. Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election. This means, in future recall elections, voters would only decide whether to remove an elected official from a state office, not who would replace the official.
Specifies Steps for Filling Vacant Offices. If a state official is recalled, Proposition 5 makes the office of the recalled official vacant. Except for the office of the Governor, Proposition 5 uses the existing process for filling vacancies to fill the office. In the case of an office in the state Senate or Assembly, this means that a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election. The Governor would choose who would fill a vacancy in any other office (other than office of the Governor).
Creates Separate Process for Filling the Office of the Governor. The process for filling the office of the Governor depends on when the recall occurs. If the Governor is recalled before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the term, Proposition 5 says that the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election. If the Governor is recalled later in the term, the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor for the rest of the term.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Fiscal Effects Depend on Frequency of Recalls and the Offices Recalled. Whether there would be costs or savings compared with today depends on the frequency of future recalls and the offices recalled. A recall of a statewide office (for example, Lieutenant Governor) would affect state elections officials and local elections officials in all 58 counties. A recall of a district-based office (for example, a state Senator or Assembly Member) would only affect state elections officials and local elections officials in those districts.
Potential Costs. Proposition 5 could result in higher costs associated with future recall elections if a special election is necessary to fill the vacant office after a recall. For example, a legislative office made vacant after a recall typically would be filled through a special election. If that special election could not be consolidated with a scheduled election, elections officials would need to run a standalone special election. The cost to state and local elections officials to administer such a special election could be millions of dollars per election.
Potential Savings. Proposition 5 could result in lower costs by removing the second question from the ballot. These savings would occur when a Governor is recalled in the latter part of the term and for other offices where vacancies are filled by appointment. There would be savings because ballots and voting materials would no longer include information about replacement candidates. The amount of savings would depend on how many candidates there would have been on the ballot if the second question remained but could be millions of dollars per election.
Net Effect Depends on Circumstances of Future Recall Efforts. The net fiscal effect is unknown because it depends on future recall elections. Proposition 5 could lead to savings or costs potentially in the range of millions of dollars to administer recall elections. How these savings or costs would be shared by state and county governments would depend on future decisions by the Legislature. This net fiscal effect represents less than one-tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)

CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 5
California’s recall process should protect our democracy by allowing for the removal of an elected official who is corrupt or abusing their power. It should never be used as a tactic to ‘redo’ an election as a political or partisan scheme. Proposition 5 will restore the recall to its original purpose by making it fair, democratic, and accountable to the will of the majority.
Under current law, a statewide recall ballot asks voters two questions in sequence:
(1) Should the official be recalled? (2) If so, who should replace them?
By being connected, these two questions create a dangerous loophole. An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority. Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast in the election. This encourages political actors to target officials they couldn’t defeat in a regular election and to install replacements who lack broad public support.
We saw this play out in the 2021 gubernatorial recall. Voters rejected it decisively. The recall lost by nearly the same number of votes that the Governor won the regular election with. But California taxpayers were forced to spend more than $200 million on an election whose outcome simply reconfirmed what voters had already decided. Nearly 70% of California likely voters called the effort a waste of taxpayer money. And had the recall succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with support from only about 28% of all recall voters.
Proposition 5 makes a single, commonsense change: it removes the second question from the recall ballot .
Under Prop. 5, in a state-level recall, voters would decide one very simple and important question: whether an officeholder should be removed. If a majority votes yes, that office becomes vacant and is filled under existing vacancy rules. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor and if the recall occurs early enough, voters would elect a replacement at the next statewide election; other statewide officers would be filled by appointment under existing rules; legislative seats by special election. No shortcuts, no loopholes, and no replacement candidate winning office without majority voter support.
In most states with recalls, vacancies are already filled by succession or a separate election, not a same-day replacement contest.
By eliminating the second question, Proposition 5 removes the incentive and ability to weaponize recalls as a shortcut for partisan advantage. Recalls could not be gamed to overturn the results of regular elections or install candidates who couldn’t win under normal conditions.
The framers of our recall process intended to safeguard voters against corrupt and unaccountable officials, not to provide a weapon for political operators to undo election results they don’t like. Proposition 5 preserves the recall as a tool for accountability while preventing it from being used to sidestep regular elections and majority rule.
Vote YES on Proposition 5 to protect majority rule, defend taxpayers, and restore California’s recall process back to the voters it was designed to serve.
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Darius L. Kemp , MPA, Executive Director
California Common Cause
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
California Fair Political Practices Commission
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 5
Disregard the mental gymnastics the other side is doing here to tie us in knots and try to make sense of the truly nonsensical.
They say Proposition 5 “protects democracy.” It does the opposite-it erodes one of the fundamental elements of our recall process: to choose who replaces the recalled politician.
That’s not protecting democracy-that’s protecting political elites.
They call California’s system a “dangerous loophole.” It’s worked for 100 years, ousting politicians who abuse their office and replacing them with whoever the voters decide will do better.
Proposition 5 would create a loophole, not close one. The other side is gaslighting you. They think you won’t notice. Don’t be fooled.
If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he raised taxes after breaking campaign promises.
Now, he wants to burn it down on his way out the door-making future recalls less effective and keeping politicians like him less accountable.
If you traded in your car, would you want to know what you were getting in return-or would you be happy to sign it away and let the salesman stick you in a jalopy of their choosing after you’ve already committed? That’s what Proposition 5 asks you to do.
Our recall system will continue to work just fine, if we don’t let political elites with sour grapes tinker with it to their benefit.
Vote NO!
Brian W. Jones , Senate Minority Leader
Joe Patterson , Assemblymember
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 will take away your voice and erode your ability to remove and replace failed or corrupt politicians from office.
California politicians already have too much power. Proposition 5 gives them even more-and it does it by taking power away from you, the voters.
For over 100 years, California’s recall process has given us the ability to remove elected officials who abuse their office, break promises or fail to do the job they were elected to do. And, when that happens, the current process allows you-not politicians-to choose who replaces them.
Proposition 5 changes that system forever and takes power away from the people.
Today, a recall election asks two simple questions: Should the elected official be removed from office? If so, who should replace them? That means Californians can remove a failed politician and immediately choose someone new to take their place.
Proposition 5 keeps the first part but eliminates your ability to vote for a replacement.
Instead, Sacramento political insiders would decide what happens next. In many cases, politicians themselves-not voters-would choose who fills the vacancy, essentially allowing them to appoint another one of their friends or political allies to replace the one you just ousted.
In other cases, rather than an immediate replacement, the seat would sit vacant until another costly election-funded by you, the taxpayer-was scheduled months later. And here’s the kicker; that failed politician you just ran out the door for failure or corruption, they'd be allowed to run in that next election to regain control of the seat they just lost.
In either case, your vote matters less, and the political establishment gains more control.
Californians deserve the right to remove an elected official-and to choose who comes next. Proposition 5 takes away half of that right, and that’s wrong.
Supporters claim this measure improves democracy. It doesn’t. Democracy means voters-not Sacramento politicians-get to choose their leaders, when to give them the boot and who to replace them with. Proposition 5 undermines that fundamental concept.
Ask yourself: if you vote to remove a governor or another statewide elected official, shouldn’t you also decide who replaces them?
The answer is clear.
It’s also worth wondering why this measure is on the ballot in the first place. Why fix a system that isn’t broken and has been working just fine for over a century?
Well, the author of this proposal himself was recalled by California voters when he voted to raise gas taxes after promising not to. Instead of respecting the will of the people, he now wants to rewrite the rules and protect politicians like him from any meaningful accountability. California’s recall belongs to the people-not politicians. Protect your voice. Protect your vote. Protect your right to hold elected officials accountable.
Vote NO on Proposition 5.
Brian W. Jones , Senate Minority Leader
Joe Patterson , Assemblymember
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 5
Don’t be misled. Proposition 5 preserves your power to recall an official by majority vote while closing the loophole that allows a replacement candidate to take office with a small fraction of the vote.
Under current law, voters decide whether to remove an official by majority vote, but the replacement can win with far less than a majority. In 2021, a replacement candidate could have become Governor with support from 28% of recall voters. That is not majority rule.
Opponents want you to believe Proposition 5 takes away your right to choose. It does not. The real question is whether someone should become Governor with support from only a small fraction of California voters.
Proposition 5 preserves the recall while separating the decision to remove an officeholder from the decision about who should serve next. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor-elected statewide by California voters-provides continuity of government until voters choose the next Governor through a regular election. Voters will still choose their elected officials. But candidates seeking statewide office should earn that office in a regular election based on their qualifications, record, and plans for California, not use a recall as a shortcut to power.
A recall should decide whether an officeholder remains in office. Choosing who governs should happen in a regular election, where candidates earn the support of California voters. Proposition 5 protects the recall, respects majority rule, and ensures candidates run on their own merits. Vote YES on Proposition 5.
